newsitem.title: USA: U.S. stocks open hinges on January jobs data.
newsitem.headline: U.S. stocks open hinges on January jobs data.

text.p: Eagerly waited January payroll and unemployment rate data will set the tone for trading on Wall Street Friday, analysts said.

Payrolls are expected to come in at 237,000 versus 262,000 in February while the unemployment rate is forecast at 5.2 percent compared with 5.3 the previous month. The data are due out at 0830 EST/1330 GMT.
"Everything depends on the numbers," said Larry Wachtel, analyst at Prudential Securities. "This is the most important number when it comes to divining what monetary policy will be."
Wachtel said the jobs data, closely monitored by the Federal Reserve, "are the hardest data to forecast because of seasonal adjustments."
He said that if the payrolls number came in below 200,000 it would rally bonds and, subsequently, stocks.

"We have have a couple of days of consolidation, and the techs are starting to come out of their slump," Wachtel said. "If the payroll number is below 200,000 it will rally the bonds, and the high techs will rally on the stock market."
In Tokyo, the Nikkei Average was down 171.39 points, or 0.95 percent, at 17,867.04.
In London, the FTSE 100 Index was up 14.8 at 4280.7.

Among U.S. shares traded in London, American Express Co was up 1/2 at$62-1/2 following press reports that the U.S. Justice Department was preparing to file an antitrust suit against VISA USA and MasterCard International for barring member banks from issuing AMEX and Discover credit cards. The Wall Street Journal reported on Friday that the suit could be filed as early as the end of the month unless VISA and MasterCard agreed to change their rules.
International Business Machines Corp , which dropped 2-3/4 in New York on Thursday, was up 3/8 at 146. Intel Corp was up 1/2 at 153-5/8.
The dollar hit new highs in Tokyo and Europe.
U.S. Treasuries were mostly higher ahead of the jobs data, with the long bond up 4/32 to yield 6.75 percent.

The Wall Street Journal's Heard on the Street writes that Sotheby's Holdings Inc suspended two employees after a British television documentary prepared to report that one of the company's traders helped smuggle a painting out of Italy.
The paper wrote that some of Wall Street's best-known investors are packing Sotheby's, bidding for profits.
The New York Times Market Place writes that Morgan Stanley Group Inc shareholders appear to be getting the better deal in the merger with Dean Witter Discover & Co.
